plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a cutaway diagram of the Frasch process for mining elemental sulfur from deep underground deposits, depicting three concentric pipes that simultaneously deliver superheated water and compressed air downward and recover liquid sulfur upward. The diagram is divided into three visible strata: an above-ground surface region, a brown soil layer, and a deep yellow solid sulfur deposit at the bottom, where a pool of liquid sulfur collects after the deposit is melted. Labeled arrows trace each fluid pathway: superheated water (170 °C, 10 atm) travels down the outermost pipe (downward arrows) and melts the surrounding sulfur; compressed air, entering from the upper right, travels down the innermost pipe; and the resulting frothy mixture of liquid sulfur, water, and air is forced up through the middle pipe (upward arrows) and exits at the surface to the upper left, labeled "Sulfur, water, and air." The three concentric pipes terminate at the bottom in a curved manifold that directs hot water outward into the deposit and channels the molten sulfur inward toward the rising middle pipe. This figure introduces the Frasch process as a purely physical extraction method that exploits sulfur's low melting point and low density, requiring no underground mining operations and yielding sulfur of 99.5–99.9% purity directly upon surface cooling.

interactionPlan.concept: The Frasch process extracts sulfur as a liquid by pumping superheated water down an outer pipe to melt the underground deposit and compressed air down an inner pipe to lift the molten sulfur froth up a middle pipe — a purely physical extraction requiring no underground mining.
elements: Vertical cutaway scene split into three horizontal strata: white above-ground region (top), brown soil layer (middle), golden-yellow solid sulfur deposit (bottom) with a lighter radial glow marking the melted pool
Three concentric pipe pairs drawn in cutaway as nested vertical outlines: outermost pipe (thick black casing walls), middle pipe, innermost narrow pipe
Curved manifold at the pipe bottoms: inner pipe ends in a U-turn, middle pipe openings face the molten pool, outer pipe discharges hot water into the deposit
Cream/pale-yellow fill inside the middle pipe representing the sulfur-water-air froth column, fading lighter toward the top
Surface wellhead assembly: stepped rectangular housing where the middle pipe opens to a side outlet on the upper left
Inlet line entering from the upper right with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Compressed air', bending down into the innermost pipe
Inlet line entering from the right at mid-height with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Superheated water', joining the outermost pipe
Outlet at the upper left with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Sulfur, water, and air'
Downward flow arrows inside the outer pipe annulus (superheated water path)
Downward flow arrow inside the innermost pipe (compressed air path)
Upward flow arrows inside the middle pipe (rising froth path)
Curved arrows at the base pointing inward/upward from the molten pool into the middle pipe, labeled 'Liquid sulfur'
Leader line and label 'Soil' pointing at the brown stratum
Label 'Solid sulfur deposit' on the yellow stratum
Annotation callouts for operating conditions: water at 170 °C and 10 atm; sulfur melts near 115 °C; product purity 99.5–99.9%
Optional inset: top-down cross-section of the three concentric pipes as three nested circles, color-coded blue (water annulus), cream (froth), grey (air)

interactions.label: Frasch process stage
interactions.teaches: The extraction is a sequence of three simultaneous but conceptually distinct fluid paths — heat down, air down, product up — and each one has a specific job.

interactions.label: Play continuous flow
interactions.teaches: In steady operation all three streams move at once: water descends the outer annulus, air descends the core, and the aerated molten sulfur climbs continuously to the wellhead.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The three 'pipes' are not side by side but concentric — one tube inside another inside another — which is why a single borehole can carry three separate streams.
Each labeled part carries its own operating condition (170 °C water, 10 atm air, ~115 °C sulfur melting point, 99.5–99.9% pure product) without cluttering the diagram with all of them at once.

demo_steps.title: The well and the deposit
demo_steps.narration: A single borehole is sunk through the soil into a solid sulfur deposit, carrying three concentric pipes. Nothing is flowing yet — the sulfur below is still solid rock-like yellow.

demo_steps.title: Three pipes, one hole
demo_steps.narration: Looking down the borehole, the pipes are nested rings: hot water travels in the outer annulus, froth returns in the middle, and compressed air goes down the narrow core.

demo_steps.title: Superheated water descends
demo_steps.narration: Water at 170 °C under about 10 atm is pumped down the outermost pipe and discharged into the deposit — pressure keeps it liquid far above its normal boiling point.

demo_steps.title: The sulfur melts
demo_steps.narration: Sulfur melts near 115 °C, so the hot water liquefies the deposit around the pipe bottom, creating a bright pool of molten sulfur — no one ever goes underground.

demo_steps.title: Compressed air goes down the core
demo_steps.narration: Air forced down the innermost pipe bubbles into the dense molten sulfur at the bottom of the middle pipe, turning it into a light, frothy mixture.

demo_steps.title: Froth rises to the surface
demo_steps.narration: Aerated sulfur is far less dense than the surrounding liquid column, so it is pushed all the way up the middle pipe and out the wellhead as sulfur, water, and air.

demo_steps.title: Pure sulfur on cooling
demo_steps.narration: At the surface the mixture separates and the sulfur solidifies at 99.5–99.9% purity — a physical separation that needs no chemical refining.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Sulfur is mined without mining: hot water melts it in place and injected air makes the melt buoyant enough to float itself up the pipe, so the entire process is a physical phase change plus a density trick.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Tall portrait diagram. Top ~55% is white above-ground space; a brown soil band occupies the middle; a golden-yellow sulfur deposit fills the bottom, with a soft pale radial glow around the pipe base marking the molten pool. Draw the well as nested vertical outlines centered horizontally: heavy black outer casing walls, a thinner middle pipe just inside, and a narrow innermost pipe at the center; fill the middle pipe with a cream-to-white vertical gradient (froth). At the bottom, the innermost pipe turns in a small U and the middle pipe openings flare toward the pool; curved arrows sweep from the pool inward and upward into the middle pipe under the label 'Liquid sulfur'. At the surface, a stepped rectangular wellhead box with a side outlet on the left carries double left-pointing arrows and the label 'Sulfur, water, and air'; on the upper right, two bent lines with left-pointing arrows are labeled 'Compressed air'; at mid-height on the right, another pair of left-pointing arrows is labeled 'Superheated water'. Use consistent arrow coding: blue-tinted down arrows in the outer annulus for water, grey down arrow in the core for air, warm amber up arrows in the middle pipe for froth. Labels 'Soil' with a leader line into the brown band and 'Solid sulfur deposit' on the yellow band. Hover callouts show 170 °C / 10 atm for water, ~115 °C melting point for sulfur, and 99.5–99.9% purity at the outlet. The cross-section view replaces the cutaway with three concentric circles color-coded to the same scheme, labeled outer = superheated water, middle = sulfur/water/air froth, inner = compressed air.

authoredContext:
The Frasch process , illustrated in , is important in the mining of free sulfur from enormous underground deposits in Texas and Louisiana. Superheated water (170 °C and 10 atm pressure) is forced down the outermost of three concentric pipes to the underground deposit. The hot water melts the sulfur. The innermost pipe conducts compressed air into the liquid sulfur. The air forces the liquid sulfur, mixed with air, to flow up through the outlet pipe. Transferring the mixture to large settling vats allows the solid sulfur to separate upon cooling. This sulfur is 99.5% to 99.9% pure and requires no purification for most uses.

The Frasch process is used to mine sulfur from underground deposits.

A diagram is shown in which a vertical tube is embedded on the lower end into a multilayered solid. The upper layer is labeled, “Soil,” and the lower layer is labeled, “Solid sulfur deposit.” A thin tube, beginning at the top of the diagram, leads into the vertical tube to the bottom and is labeled, “Compressed air.” Left-facing and then down-facing arrows are drawn on this inner tube. These arrows then turn upward at the bottom of the tube and are drawn upward to indicate the flow of, “Liquid sulfur,” from the bottom of the diagram to the top outside the inner tube. These arrows lead to a chamber at the top right of the diagram with arrows facing to the left labeled, “Sulfur, water and air.” A horizontal tube in the center right of the diagram leads to the outer tube and arrows drawn downward lead back to the bottom of the diagram. This tube is labeled, “Superheated water.”

Larger amounts of sulfur also come from hydrogen sulfide recovered during the purification of natural gas.

discrepancies: Label type size is noticeably smaller relative to the artwork than in the source (source labels are large and dominant; here they render at roughly 11 px inline), weakening the hierarchy the original establishes.

The per-phase annotation text block is drawn in the left whitespace starting at x=24 with lines up to ~20 characters; on steps like 'froth rises' / 'compressed air down' it can run into the outer pipe outline at x≈218, a collision not present in the source.

Bottom-of-well detail differs slightly: the source shows two distinct U-turn pipe tips with a clearly open annulus discharge, while the generated version renders shorter, more schematic U-bends and adds a molten-pool ellipse (appears in later steps) not present in the source.

Extra chrome not in the source: colour-coded stream legend, animated particle dots and the cross-section circle view (behind a toggle) — acceptable as interaction layers but they change the palette away from the source's all-black arrows once a later phase is selected.
'Solid sulfur deposit' sits very close to the right edge of the artboard and to the black casing, tighter than the comfortable placement in the source.
evaluation.notes: A close, well-composed reproduction of the Frasch-process cutaway with correct pipe topology, strata colours, arrow directions and all source labels, backed by a genuinely useful 7-step walkthrough, phase selector, cross-section toggle and flow animation; main weaknesses are undersized label type versus the source and a phase-annotation block that can collide with the well outline.
action_items: Increase label font size (e.g. 30–34 in viewbox units) so the primary callouts read as prominently as in the source at inline scale, and keep a clear size hierarchy between the main callouts and the smaller phase annotations.
Reposition or wrap the phase-annotation lines (shorter lines, or move them below the wellhead in clear whitespace) so they never overlap the outer pipe outline at x≈218.
Nudge 'Solid sulfur deposit' inward from the right edge and add a little clearance from the black casing bar.
Refine the bottom U-turn geometry (longer tails, clearer annulus discharge gap) to match the source's pipe-foot detail more closely.

feedback.rationale: Concept, structure, and interaction design are sound (concept 5, no failure modes, no plan action items); remaining issues are implementation details like font sizing, text collisions, and pipe-foot geometry.

The source repeats several flow arrows within each pipe segment (e.g. two stacked up-arrows in the froth pipe above and below the soil line, two down-arrows in each annulus); the generated version uses fewer, longer single arrows, so arrow density/rhythm differs.

Added elements not in the source: an optional concentric pipe cross-section view (behind a checkbox) and a small cream annotation card in the left whitespace that appears from step 3 onward — legitimate teaching additions but extra chrome relative to the static original.

Because the 660×1295 portrait viewbox is fitted by height in a landscape container, the rendered artwork is only ~285 px wide, making the 30–32 px callout text render at roughly 13–14 px; legible but noticeably tighter than the prominent labels in the source.

The bottom 'Liquid sulfur' curved arrows are shorter/straighter than the source's long sweeping curves into the melt pool, and the central discharge gap between the U-feet is smaller than in the original.

Three concentric pipe pairs drawn in cutaway as nested vertical outlines: outermost pipe (thick black casing walls), middle pipe, innermost narrow pipe
Curved manifold at the pipe bottoms: inner pipe ends in a U-turn, middle pipe openings face the molten pool, outer pipe discharges hot water into the deposit
Cream/pale-yellow fill inside the middle pipe representing the sulfur-water-air froth column, fading lighter toward the top
Surface wellhead assembly: stepped rectangular housing where the middle pipe opens to a side outlet on the upper left
Inlet line entering from the upper right with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Compressed air', bending down into the innermost pipe
Inlet line entering from the right at mid-height with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Superheated water', joining the outermost pipe
Outlet at the upper left with left-pointing double arrows, labeled 'Sulfur, water, and air'
Downward flow arrows inside the outer pipe annulus (superheated water path)
Downward flow arrow inside the innermost pipe (compressed air path)
Upward flow arrows inside the middle pipe (rising froth path)
Curved arrows at the base pointing inward/upward from the molten pool into the middle pipe, labeled 'Liquid sulfur'
Leader line and label 'Soil' pointing at the brown stratum
Label 'Solid sulfur deposit' on the yellow stratum
Annotation callouts for operating conditions: water at 170 °C and 10 atm; sulfur melts near 115 °C; product purity 99.5–99.9%
Optional inset: top-down cross-section of the three concentric pipes as three nested circles, color-coded blue (water annulus), cream (froth), grey (air)

interactions.label: Frasch process stage
interactions.teaches: The extraction is a sequence of three simultaneous but conceptually distinct fluid paths — heat down, air down, product up — and each one has a specific job.

interactions.label: Play continuous flow
interactions.teaches: In steady operation all three streams move at once: water descends the outer annulus, air descends the core, and the aerated molten sulfur climbs continuously to the wellhead.

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The three 'pipes' are not side by side but concentric — one tube inside another inside another — which is why a single borehole can carry three separate streams.
Each labeled part carries its own operating condition (170 °C water, 10 atm air, ~115 °C sulfur melting point, 99.5–99.9% pure product) without cluttering the diagram with all of them at once.

demo_steps.title: The well and the deposit
demo_steps.narration: A single borehole is sunk through the soil into a solid sulfur deposit, carrying three concentric pipes. Nothing is flowing yet — the sulfur below is still solid rock-like yellow.

demo_steps.title: Three pipes, one hole
demo_steps.narration: Looking down the borehole, the pipes are nested rings: hot water travels in the outer annulus, froth returns in the middle, and compressed air goes down the narrow core.

demo_steps.title: Superheated water descends
demo_steps.narration: Water at 170 °C under about 10 atm is pumped down the outermost pipe and discharged into the deposit — pressure keeps it liquid far above its normal boiling point.

demo_steps.title: The sulfur melts
demo_steps.narration: Sulfur melts near 115 °C, so the hot water liquefies the deposit around the pipe bottom, creating a bright pool of molten sulfur — no one ever goes underground.

demo_steps.title: Compressed air goes down the core
demo_steps.narration: Air forced down the innermost pipe bubbles into the dense molten sulfur at the bottom of the middle pipe, turning it into a light, frothy mixture.

demo_steps.title: Froth rises to the surface
demo_steps.narration: Aerated sulfur is far less dense than the surrounding liquid column, so it is pushed all the way up the middle pipe and out the wellhead as sulfur, water, and air.

demo_steps.title: Pure sulfur on cooling
demo_steps.narration: At the surface the mixture separates and the sulfur solidifies at 99.5–99.9% purity — a physical separation that needs no chemical refining.

plan.keyInsight: Sulfur is mined without mining: hot water melts it in place and injected air makes the melt buoyant enough to float itself up the pipe, so the entire process is a physical phase change plus a density trick.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Tall portrait diagram. Top ~55% is white above-ground space; a brown soil band occupies the middle; a golden-yellow sulfur deposit fills the bottom, with a soft pale radial glow around the pipe base marking the molten pool. Draw the well as nested vertical outlines centered horizontally: heavy black outer casing walls, a thinner middle pipe just inside, and a narrow innermost pipe at the center; fill the middle pipe with a cream-to-white vertical gradient (froth). At the bottom, the innermost pipe turns in a small U and the middle pipe openings flare toward the pool; curved arrows sweep from the pool inward and upward into the middle pipe under the label 'Liquid sulfur'. At the surface, a stepped rectangular wellhead box with a side outlet on the left carries double left-pointing arrows and the label 'Sulfur, water, and air'; on the upper right, two bent lines with left-pointing arrows are labeled 'Compressed air'; at mid-height on the right, another pair of left-pointing arrows is labeled 'Superheated water'. Use consistent arrow coding: blue-tinted down arrows in the outer annulus for water, grey down arrow in the core for air, warm amber up arrows in the middle pipe for froth. Labels 'Soil' with a leader line into the brown band and 'Solid sulfur deposit' on the yellow band. Hover callouts show 170 °C / 10 atm for water, ~115 °C melting point for sulfur, and 99.5–99.9% purity at the outlet. The cross-section view replaces the cutaway with three concentric circles color-coded to the same scheme, labeled outer = superheated water, middle = sulfur/water/air froth, inner = compressed air.

discrepancies: Label sizing hierarchy differs from the source: 'Solid sulfur deposit' (and the cross-section callouts) are rendered smaller than the other primary callouts, whereas the source uses one consistent label size for all callouts.

'Compressed air' is placed to the left of and below its inlet arrows (nearer the wellhead) rather than under/right of the two inflow arrows as in the source, slightly weakening the arrow→label association.

The generated figure adds elements not in the source: a left-margin stage annotation card, coloured (blue/grey/gold) flow arrows in non-default stages, animated particles, and a full pipe cross-section panel — enrichment, but it changes the look away from the source's uniformly black arrows once a stage is chosen.
Minor proportion drift: the molten-sulfur glow/pool and the curved 'Liquid sulfur' intake arrows are shorter and flatter than the source's long sweeping curves rising into the middle pipe.
evaluation.notes: A close, well-composed reproduction of the Frasch-process well cutaway with correct three-pipe topology, strata, arrow directions and all source labels, backed by genuinely useful stage stepping, cross-section toggle and flow animation; weaknesses are minor label-size inconsistency, a slightly displaced 'Compressed air' label, and added chrome (annotation card, coloured arrows) that drifts from the source's uniform black-arrow styling.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes or action items remain and all dimensions score 4-5 with correct concept and interactions, so remaining issues are cosmetic nitpicks not worth another iteration.
